nodes.text: Neural retrieval models are usually trained and evaluated on a single dataset/domain, so it is unclear how they perform on new tasks and domains without in-domain training data.

Building labeled training data for every new retrieval domain is costly and slow, so many real applications must apply a retriever zero-shot; if generalization is poor, this is discovered only in deployment.
Prior work trained retrievers on large in-domain sets such as MS MARCO or Natural Questions and reported large gains over BM25, but evaluated on the same, single dataset.
The two existing broad-coverage retrieval evaluations, MultiReQA and KILT, each cover only one task type and lean heavily on Wikipedia-derived, often small, corpora.

Neither MultiReQA nor KILT shows how different retrieval architectures compare when generalizing zero-shot across many tasks and domains at once, so it is unknown whether in-domain neural gains transfer out of domain.

RQ1: How well, and via which architectural mechanisms, do ten representative retrieval systems from five architecture families generalize zero-shot across diverse tasks and domains, relative to the lexical baseline BM25?
Construct a heterogeneous, standardized zero-shot benchmark and use it to compare systems spanning lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction and re-ranking architectures.

Select 18 datasets across 9 tasks by four criteria (diverse tasks, diverse domains, sufficient difficulty, diverse annotation strategies); unify them into one data format; score every system with one metric, nDCG@10.
Evaluate all ten systems zero-shot on all 18 datasets plus in-domain MS MARCO; profile latency and index size on a 1M-document DBPedia sample.

BM25 remains a strong zero-shot baseline; no architecture dominates; re-ranking and late-interaction generalize best but are slowest and largest; several dense and sparse-reweighting systems underperform BM25 on average.

In-domain accuracy does not predict zero-shot generalization; robust generalization here is more closely associated with cross-attention(-like) query-document interaction than with embedding architecture alone, and it costs more compute and memory.

If several BEIR test collections were pooled predominantly from lexical retrieval systems, non-lexical systems' apparent underperformance in the RQ1 comparison may be partly a measurement artifact rather than a true capability gap.

Retrieval test-collection annotation pools are built from the candidates that some existing system(s) retrieve; unseen candidates are assumed irrelevant, which is a documented source of selection bias in IR evaluation, and several BEIR datasets (BioASQ, Signal-1M) are known to have been pooled using lexical term-matching.
RQ2: Do existing pooling/annotation practices for retrieval test collections systematically disadvantage non-lexical systems in a way that affects the RQ1 comparison?

Case study on TREC-COVID: compute each system's Hole@10 (share of top-10 hits never judged), then manually annotate the 980 previously-unjudged pairs, blind to which system retrieved them, and recompute nDCG@10.

Lexical systems have low Hole@10 and change little after re-annotation; non-lexical systems have much higher Hole@10 and improve substantially (ANCE +8.1 points, ColBERT +5.8 points) after re-annotation.

Current pooling practice for at least some BEIR test collections is lexically biased and understates non-lexical systems' true zero-shot performance; the RQ1 ranking on such datasets should be read with this in mind.

BEIR: a standardized, open-source, 18-dataset/9-task zero-shot IR benchmark; a large comparative study of 10 systems across 5 architecture families showing BM25's robustness and a generalization/cost trade-off; and a documented annotation-bias case study that should inform future test-collection design.

The benchmark's coverage is bounded: English-only text, mostly short-to-medium documents (transformer 512-wordpiece truncation), pure textual signals only, and only one or two document fields. (Detailed as L001-L004 in claims/claim_evidence_map.json.)

The comparison targets models built to generalize broadly; a task-specific specialized model could still beat the generalist systems compared here on one task. No error bars are available for the individual comparisons, and total compute used is not fully reported. (Detailed as L005-L007 in claims/claim_evidence_map.json.)

The annotation-bias measurement (Hole@10 and re-annotation) was carried out on one dataset, TREC-COVID; its exact size elsewhere in BEIR is argued by analogy, not separately measured. (Detailed as L008 in claims/claim_evidence_map.json.)

Retrieval research should report zero-shot/cross-domain results, not only in-domain metrics, using benchmarks such as BEIR; future test-collection builders should diversify pooling across architecture types.

Extend to multilingual/cross-lingual datasets, long-document retrieval, non-textual ranking signals, multi-field retrieval, an actively maintained public leaderboard, and more diverse annotation pooling for new test collections.
Zero-shot (out-of-domain) retrieval: applying a retriever to a task/domain it received no training data for.
nodes.audience_note: Define at first use for mode B; adjacent researchers know 'zero-shot' generally but not its specific meaning for retrieval corpora/query types.

nodes.text: Retrieval architecture taxonomy used throughout: lexical (token overlap, e.g. BM25), sparse (learned term weights/expansions on top of lexical matching), dense (single-vector embedding similarity), late-interaction (multiple token-level embeddings compared at query time), re-ranking (a cross-attention model re-scores a first-stage candidate list).
nodes.audience_note: Core background for the whole paper; introduce before the first result.

nodes.text: nDCG@10: a graded, rank-position-aware retrieval metric that credits relevant documents more when they appear higher in the top 10 results.
nodes.audience_note: Adjacent researchers likely know ranking metrics exist but not this one specifically.

nodes.text: BM25: a classical bag-of-words scoring function that ranks documents by weighted term overlap with the query, with no learned parameters.
nodes.audience_note: Needed before any comparison 'against BM25' is meaningful.

nodes.text: Pooling: because manually judging every (query, document) pair is infeasible, test collections are built by judging only the top candidates returned by some existing system(s); everything else is assumed irrelevant.
nodes.audience_note: Needed before RQ2/the bias case study makes sense.

experiment_chains.experiment: EXP1: 18-dataset zero-shot comparison of 10 retrieval systems
experiment_chains.hypothesis: No stated single falsifiable hypothesis; the objective is a comprehensive comparison. Implicit expectation entering the study: neural systems that beat BM25 in-domain will also beat it out-of-domain.
experiment_chains.falsifier: Some systems that beat BM25 in-domain underperform it out-of-domain, and architectures with more capacity/parameters do not automatically generalize better.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: One shared data format and metric (nDCG@10) makes the ten systems' scores directly comparable across all 18 datasets, isolating architecture-related differences in generalization from dataset-specific measurement differences.
experiment_chains.next: The main comparison ranks several non-lexical systems below BM25 on many datasets; because several of these datasets' relevance judgements were pooled largely from lexical systems (N28), the next question is whether that ranking is partly a measurement artifact (EXP2).

experiment_chains.experiment: EXP2: TREC-COVID annotation-pool bias case study
experiment_chains.hypothesis: Non-lexical systems' top-10 hits are judged by the existing annotation pool at a lower rate than lexical systems' hits are, because the pool was built with help from lexical retrieval.
experiment_chains.falsifier: Hole@10 rates and score changes after re-annotation are similar across lexical and non-lexical systems.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: Measuring Hole@10 shows how much of each system's output the existing judgements can even evaluate; manually completing the missing judgements, blind to the retrieving system, isolates the pooling artifact from any other difference between systems.
